pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Predict the impact of changes in electrical circuits with regards to the output of bulbs, and describe how electrical energy transformation occurs in series and parallel circuits.
- Construct simple electrical circuits and measure the voltage, current and resistance.
- Calculate the potential difference in a circuit using the formula V = IR, where I is the current and R is the resistance.

pages.title: Electrical Energy Transformation in a Circuit
pages.body: An electrical circuit is a complete path along which electric current can flow, and whenever current flows through a component such as a bulb, buzzer or motor, electrical energy is transformed into another useful form, light and heat in a bulb, sound in a buzzer, or motion in a motor. Building a circuit and observing this transformation directly connects the abstract idea of electrical energy to something visible, audible, or otherwise directly observable.

pages.title: Series Circuits
pages.body: A series circuit connects components one after another along a single path, so that the same current flows through every component in turn, with no alternative route available. If one component in a series circuit fails or is removed, the entire circuit is broken, and every other component stops working, since there is no other path for current to take. Adding more bulbs in series generally makes each bulb glow more dimly, since the same total voltage from the source is shared across a greater number of components.

pages.title: Parallel Circuits
pages.body:
A parallel circuit connects components along separate branches, so that current has more than one possible path to follow, with each branch effectively receiving the same voltage from the source. If one component in a parallel circuit fails or is removed, current can still flow through the other branches, so the remaining components continue working normally, unlike in a series circuit. Adding more bulbs in parallel generally does not dim the existing bulbs, since each branch still receives close to the full source voltage, though it does increase the total current drawn from the source.

[[pic:Two labelled circuit diagrams side by side, the first showing a battery connected to three bulbs arranged one after another along a single loop, labelled Series Circuit, and the second showing a battery connected to three bulbs arranged on three separate parallel branches, labelled Parallel Circuit, with a small inset note under each showing what happens to the remaining bulbs if one bulb is removed.]]

Notice that removing one bulb in the series circuit breaks the entire loop, switching off all the bulbs, while removing one bulb in the parallel circuit only affects that particular branch, leaving the other bulbs lit, which is why household wiring is generally designed using a parallel arrangement.

lessons.title: Constructing a Simple Circuit and Measuring Its Properties

pages.title: Constructing a Simple Circuit and Measuring Its Properties
pages.body: A simple circuit can be constructed using a battery, connecting wires, a bulb or resistor, and a switch, arranged in a complete loop. A voltmeter, connected across a component, measures the potential difference (voltage) across that component, while an ammeter, connected in series within the circuit, measures the current flowing through it. Careful, correct connection of these measuring instruments is essential, since a voltmeter and an ammeter are connected differently within a circuit to obtain accurate readings.

pages.title: Calculating Potential Difference Using V = IR
pages.body: The potential difference across a component in a circuit can be calculated using the formula V equals I multiplied by R, where V is potential difference in volts, I is current in amperes, and R is resistance in ohms. For example, if a current of 2 amperes flows through a resistor with a resistance of 5 ohms, the potential difference across that resistor is calculated as V equals 2 multiplied by 5, giving V equals 10 volts. This formula, sometimes called Ohm's Law, allows any one of the three quantities, voltage, current or resistance, to be calculated if the other two are known.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Household electrical wiring is designed using parallel circuits precisely because this allows different appliances and lights to be switched on and off independently, without affecting the operation of other devices in the home, and without every device dimming as more devices are added, unlike what would happen if an entire house were wired in a single series circuit.

lessons.title: Forward and Reverse Bias in Electronic Circuits

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Explain forward bias and reverse bias in an electronic circuit.
- Construct different electronic circuits (the forward and reverse bias), and observe what happens to the LED.
- Construct different electronic circuits involving resistors and capacitors, and observe what happens to the LED and report on your findings.

pages.title: What is a Diode?
pages.body: A diode is an electronic component that allows current to flow through it easily in only one direction, while strongly resisting current flow in the opposite direction. This one directional behaviour makes diodes useful for controlling the direction of current in a circuit, and a light emitting diode, commonly called an LED, is a special type of diode that also emits light when current flows through it in its allowed direction.

pages.title: Forward Bias
pages.body: Forward bias describes the arrangement of a diode within a circuit where it is connected in the direction that allows current to flow through it easily. When a diode, or an LED, is connected in forward bias, with the battery's positive terminal connected in a way that matches the diode's allowed direction of flow, current flows through the component, and in the case of an LED, the LED lights up.

pages.title: Reverse Bias
pages.body:
Reverse bias describes the arrangement of a diode within a circuit where it is connected in the opposite direction, blocking the easy flow of current. When a diode, or an LED, is connected in reverse bias, current is prevented from flowing through the component in any significant amount, and in the case of an LED, the LED does not light up, since almost no current can pass through it in this arrangement.

[[pic:Two labelled circuit diagrams side by side, the first showing a battery, resistor and LED connected in forward bias, with an arrow showing current flowing through the LED and the LED drawn glowing, and the second showing the same components connected in reverse bias, with a crossed out arrow showing current blocked and the LED drawn unlit.]]

Notice that the only difference between the two circuits is the direction the LED is connected relative to the battery, yet this single difference determines whether the LED lights up or remains dark, directly demonstrating the one directional behaviour of a diode.

pages.title: Resistors in an Electronic Circuit
pages.body: A resistor is a component that limits, or resists, the flow of current through a circuit, and is commonly connected in series with an LED specifically to prevent too much current from flowing through the LED, which could otherwise damage it. Adding a resistor to an LED circuit generally makes the LED glow at a safe, controlled brightness rather than burning out from excessive current.

pages.title: Capacitors in an Electronic Circuit
pages.body: A capacitor is a component that stores electrical energy temporarily and releases it gradually, rather than allowing current to flow through it continuously in the way a plain wire would. When a capacitor is connected in a circuit with an LED, the LED may light up briefly as the capacitor charges, then dim and go out as the capacitor becomes fully charged, or light up gradually and fade slowly as the capacitor discharges, depending on how the circuit is arranged, illustrating how capacitors influence current flow differently from resistors.

questions.e: Capacitors in an Electronic Circuit A capacitor is a component that stores electrical energy temporarily and releases it gradually, rather than allowing current to flow through it continuously in the way a plain wire would.

pages.title: The Relationship Among These Components
pages.body: LEDs, diodes, resistors and capacitors each play a distinct but related role within an electronic circuit. The diode, or LED, controls the direction current is allowed to flow, the resistor controls how much current is allowed to flow, protecting sensitive components such as the LED, and the capacitor controls how current flow changes over time, storing and releasing energy gradually rather than instantly. Together, these components allow circuit designers to build electronic devices with carefully controlled, safe, and often quite sophisticated behaviour, well beyond what a simple circuit of just a battery and a bulb could achieve.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

LEDs are now widely used in place of traditional incandescent bulbs for lighting, since they convert a much greater proportion of electrical energy into light rather than wasted heat, connecting this lesson directly back to the energy efficient appliances discussed in the energy conservation lessons earlier in this strand.
